A number you cannot trace is stated as unconfirmed, not stated firmly.
AI can invent a plausible figure and it will read exactly like a real one.
Once you say it aloud it is your number, whoever produced it.

cards.headline: Build a one-page brief for your next real meeting
cards.body: Take the next meeting in your calendar that you have not prepared for. Gather the invitation, the most recent thread and any attached document, and produce a one-page brief with four sections: the decision to be reached, the background, your position with reasoning, and the one question you need answered. Then do the two things the tool cannot: write in the unwritten history yourself — what was already agreed, who is invested in what — and open the source for every figure in the brief to confirm it before you use it. Take that page into the meeting.
bullets: "Here is a meeting invitation, the latest email thread and the attached document. Give me a one-page brief with four sections: the decision this meeting has to reach, the background needed to follow it, my position with the reasoning, and the single question I must get answered. Mark anything you are unsure about, quote the source sentence for every figure, and do not invent a number or a decision that is not in what I gave you."
Add the unwritten history yourself — the tool cannot see it.
Open the source and confirm every figure before you take the page in.

quiz.question: What are the four parts of a useful meeting brief?
options: The decision to reach, the background, your position, your one question
A summary of every document attached
quiz.explanation: A brief exists so you know what the meeting must decide and what you want from it. A topic summary tells you what the meeting is about, which you already knew from the invitation.

quiz.question: What can a tool never supply in a meeting brief?
options: The unwritten history and who is invested in what
A summary of an attached document
quiz.explanation: AI cannot know what the room already agreed in a conversation nobody recorded, or which option was rejected last quarter and why. That context is what decides most meetings, so you add it yourself.

quiz.question: A figure in your brief can be quoted in the meeting without opening the source.
quiz.explanation: A number lifted from a summary, or invented, sounds exactly like one you calculated. Once you say it aloud it is yours and it gets repeated, so verify every figure before you say it in the room.

lessons.title: Never Lose a Meeting Action Again
lessons.subtitle: Capture decisions and owned actions from a live meeting — with consent, and with every name and number checked.

cards.headline: The meeting was fine, the follow-through was not
cards.body: Most meetings end with everyone agreeing and nobody owning anything. A week later two people believe the other was doing it and the work has not started. Notes are not the problem; ownership is. A meeting record is only useful if every action has a person and a date attached, and that is a discipline the tool can support but cannot supply for you.
cards.statLabel: an owner and a date, on every action

cards.headline: Ask for consent before you record anything
cards.body: A recording or transcript captures colleagues and clients saying things they assumed were unrecorded, and in many places recording without telling people is unlawful as well as unwelcome. So ask for consent before recording, say what the recording is for and where it will be stored, and check what your organisation allows before you switch anything on. If someone objects, take written notes instead — a meeting nobody trusts is worse than a meeting nobody transcribed.
bullets: Ask for consent before recording, every time, out loud at the start.
Say what it is for and where it will be stored.
Check what your organisation allows before you switch recording on.
If anyone objects, take notes instead and say so.

cards.headline: An action without an owner and a date is not an action
cards.body: Ask specifically for decisions reached and actions with a named owner and a date, and reject anything vague: "the team will look into it" is a sentence, not a commitment. Where the meeting genuinely did not assign an owner, record it as unassigned rather than guessing — an invented owner is worse than a visible gap, because the person named never agreed and never finds out. An action without an owner and a date is not an action.
bullets: An action without an owner and a date is not an action.
"The team will look into it" is recorded as unassigned, not as an action.
Never let the tool guess who owns something nobody claimed.
Separate decisions from actions, and keep both lists short.

cards.headline: A transcript can mishear a name, a number or a decision
cards.body: Automatic notes are approximations. An AI transcript can mishear a name, a number or a decision — a client becomes a colleague, fifteen becomes fifty, and "we are not doing that yet" loses the "not". Nothing flags it, because the sentence still reads naturally, and the error then travels in the follow-up email as though the meeting had said it. So read the record against your own memory before you send it, correct names and figures by hand, and circulate it so the room can challenge anything you got wrong.
bullets: An AI transcript can mishear a name, a number or a decision.
Check names and figures by hand before the record goes anywhere.
A dropped negative reverses a decision and still reads naturally.
Circulate the record so the room can correct it while they remember.

cards.headline: Capture your next real meeting properly
cards.body: Do this on the next meeting you attend. Before it starts, check what your organisation allows and ask for consent before recording; if anyone objects, take notes instead. Afterwards, turn the notes or transcript into two short lists: decisions reached, and actions with a named owner and a date, marking anything unassigned as unassigned rather than guessing. Then read it against your own memory, correct every name and number by hand, and send it to everyone who was there with an invitation to correct it. Keep the corrected version — that document is the output of this lesson.
bullets: "Here are my notes from a meeting. Give me two lists: the decisions actually reached, and the actions with a named owner and a date for each. If the meeting did not name an owner or a date, write unassigned rather than guessing, and do not invent a decision or a figure that is not in my notes. Quote the words each decision came from."
Ask for consent before recording, and check what your organisation allows.
Correct names and figures by hand, then circulate it for challenge.

quiz.question: Before recording or transcribing a meeting, what must you do?
options: Ask for consent and check what your organisation allows
Store it in a private folder
quiz.explanation: A recording captures colleagues and clients saying things they assumed were unrecorded, and in many places recording without telling people is unlawful. Consent first, and notes instead if anyone objects.

quiz.question: The meeting agreed something but named nobody. How is it recorded?
options: As unassigned, with the decision noted
Assigned to whoever spoke most about it
quiz.explanation: An invented owner is worse than a visible gap: the person named never agreed and may never find out. Recording it as unassigned keeps the gap in front of the room where it can be closed.

quiz.question: An automatic transcript can be circulated without checking names and figures.
quiz.explanation: A transcript can mishear a name or a number, or drop a negative so a decision reverses, and the sentence still reads naturally. The error then travels in the follow-up as though the meeting said it.

lessons.title: Catch Up on What You Missed
lessons.subtitle: Get back into a project or a channel quickly — without mistaking a recap for a decision record.

cards.headline: Two days away, four hundred messages
cards.body: Coming back from leave or joining a project already in motion is the same task: find the small number of things that changed, and the smaller number that need you. Scrolling is the slow way and it still misses things, because the important message is rarely the longest one. A recap gets you oriented in minutes — as long as you treat it as orientation rather than as the record of what was agreed.
cards.statLabel: what changed, what needs me, what is still open

cards.headline: Ask what changed, what needs you, what is open
cards.body: Three questions get you back in: what has changed since you were last across this, what needs something from you, and what is still open with nobody driving it. Ask for each as a short list with the date and the person attached. In Teams, Copilot can recap a channel or a chat it has access to; on a browser tool you paste in the thread or the notes. Resist asking for "a summary of the project" — that produces a paragraph you cannot act on.
bullets: Three lists: what changed, what needs you, what is still open.
Every item carries a date and a person, or it is not actionable.
Ask for the last thing decided, not a general project overview.
A recap you cannot act on is a paragraph, not a catch-up.

cards.headline: A recap tells you what was said, not what was agreed
cards.body: This is the trap that makes catching up dangerous rather than merely incomplete. A recap tells you what was said, not what was agreed: a suggestion someone made in passing appears alongside a firm decision, in the same flat voice, with nothing marking which was which. You then act on the suggestion as though the project had chosen it. So never treat a recap as a decision record — before you act, find the message or the meeting note where the decision was actually made, and read it.
bullets: A recap tells you what was said, not what was agreed.
Never treat a recap as a decision record — find the source before acting.
A passing suggestion and a firm decision read identically in a recap.
Ask it to quote the message each decision came from so you can check it.

cards.headline: Confirm anything assigned to you with the person who assigned it
cards.body: The worst version of this is an action you inherit from a recap. Something was allocated to you while you were away — or the tool decided it was yours because your name appeared nearby — and you either start work nobody wanted or discover the real deadline was last week. So check any action assigned to you with the person who assigned it, in one short message. It takes a minute, it puts the date beyond doubt, and it tells the other person you have picked it up.
bullets: Check any action assigned to you with the person who assigned it.
Confirm the date as well as the task; a recap often guesses at both.
A name appearing near an action does not mean that person owns it.
One short message removes a week of working on the wrong thing.

cards.headline: Catch up on a real channel or project
cards.body: Pick a channel, chat or project you are genuinely behind on. Produce three lists from it: what has changed since you last looked, what needs something from you with a date, and what is still open with nobody driving it. Then do the verification, which is the point of the lesson: for every decision in the recap, open the message it came from and read it in full, and for every action assigned to you, send one short message to the person who assigned it confirming the task and the date. Act on the top item before you close the lesson.
bullets: "Here is a project channel I have been away from. Give me three lists: what has changed and when, what needs something from me with dates, and what is still open with nobody driving it. Quote the message each decision came from, mark anything that was only a suggestion as a suggestion, and do not invent an owner or a date that nobody stated."
Open the source message for every decision before you act on it.
Confirm anything assigned to you with the person who assigned it.

quiz.question: What three lists get you back into a project fastest?
options: What changed, what needs you, what is still open
quiz.explanation: Those three questions produce something you can act on, each item with a date and a person. A general project overview reads well and tells you nothing to do next.

quiz.question: Why is a recap not a decision record?
options: A passing suggestion and a firm decision appear in the same flat voice
It only covers the last day
quiz.explanation: Nothing in a recap marks which items were actually decided, so you can act on a suggestion as though the project had chosen it. Find the source message and read it before you commit.

quiz.question: An action a recap assigns to you can be started without checking with anyone.
quiz.explanation: A recap can attach your name to something nobody allocated to you, or guess at the deadline. One short message to the person who assigned it confirms the task and the date.

lessons.title: Module 5 Checkpoint: Meeting to Owned Plan
lessons.subtitle: Prepare one real meeting, capture it properly, and confirm every action with the person who owns it.

cards.headline: End this lesson with a plan somebody owns
cards.body: Module 5 covered three things: preparing so you arrive knowing what the meeting must decide, capturing decisions and owned actions rather than notes, and getting back into work you missed without acting on the wrong thing. This checkpoint asks you to run all three on a real meeting in your own week, and to finish holding a brief, a record and a set of confirmed actions rather than a page of advice about meetings.
cards.statLabel: a brief, a record, confirmed actions

cards.headline: The order, and where it usually goes wrong
cards.body: Prepare, capture, then confirm. The common failure is skipping straight to capture: without a brief you do not know what the meeting was supposed to decide, so you record a conversation instead of an outcome. The second is sending the record and treating that as follow-through — circulating a list is not the same as anyone accepting an item on it. The confirmation step is what turns a document into work somebody is actually doing.
bullets: Prepare first, or you capture a conversation instead of an outcome.
Circulating a list is not the same as anyone accepting an item on it.
Confirmation is what turns a record into work in progress.

cards.headline: The three protections that carry the module
cards.body: Each of these prevents a failure that leaves no trace at the time. A recording captures people who assumed they were unrecorded, so ask for consent before recording. A tidy list of vague commitments looks like a plan and delivers nothing, so remember an action without an owner and a date is not an action. And a catch-up presents a passing suggestion in the same voice as a firm decision, so never treat a recap as a decision record. None of the three produces an error at the time; all three produce a problem you meet later.
bullets: Ask for consent before recording, and check what your organisation allows.
An action without an owner and a date is not an action.
Never treat a recap as a decision record — read the source first.

cards.headline: What stays your decision
cards.body: Two things never move to the tool. The unwritten history is the first: AI cannot know what the room already agreed off the record, or who has staked something on the current approach, so you supply that before you rely on any brief. Accuracy of names and numbers is the second: a transcript can mishear a figure or drop a negative, and the sentence still reads naturally, so you check those by hand before a record leaves your hands.
bullets: You supply the unwritten history; the tool cannot see it.
You check names and figures by hand before the record circulates.
Mechanical capture to the tool, judgement and accuracy to you.

cards.headline: One meeting, prepared, captured and confirmed
cards.body: Use a real meeting in the next few days, not an example. First, build the one-page brief: the decision to be reached, the background, your position, and your one question — then add the unwritten history yourself and verify every figure against its source before you go in. Second, in the meeting, ask for consent before recording, and afterwards produce two lists: decisions reached, and actions with a named owner and a date, marking anything nobody claimed as unassigned. Correct every name and number by hand. Third, send the record to the room and message each owner to confirm their action and its date. Keep the brief and the confirmed record: those two documents are the proof this module worked.
bullets: "Here are my notes from a meeting I prepared for. Give me two lists: the decisions actually reached, and the actions with a named owner and a date. Write unassigned where the meeting named nobody, quote the words each decision came from, and do not invent an owner, a date or a figure that is not in my notes."
Ask for consent before recording, and check what your organisation allows.
Message each owner to confirm the action and the date before you call it done.

quiz.question: What is the right order for getting value out of a meeting?
options: Capture, then prepare for the next one
Prepare, capture, then confirm each action with its owner
Record everything and read it later
Send a recap and wait for replies
quiz.explanation: Without a brief you capture a conversation rather than an outcome, and without confirmation a circulated list is not work anybody has accepted.

quiz.question: Which of these is the honest way to record something nobody claimed?
options: Mark it unassigned so the gap stays visible
Leave it out of the record
Assign it to whoever raised it
quiz.explanation: An invented owner is worse than a visible gap, because the person named never agreed and may never find out. Unassigned keeps the gap in front of the room where it can be closed.

quiz.question: A recap of a channel is a reliable record of what the project decided.
quiz.explanation: A recap tells you what was said, not what was agreed: a passing suggestion appears in the same flat voice as a firm decision. Read the source message before you act on either.

lessons.title: Build a Complete Business Report
lessons.subtitle: Take one set of numbers all the way to a document, a deck and a covering email — with every figure still traceable at the end.

cards.headline: One set of numbers, four handoffs
cards.body: A monthly or quarterly report is not one task, it is a chain: the numbers become an insight, the insight becomes a document, the document becomes a short deck, and the deck goes out with a covering email. Every step so far in this course was one link. This lesson joins them, and the joining is where the risk moves — because a figure that changed shape at the first handoff arrives at the last one looking like a fact nobody needs to check.
cards.statLabel: numbers, document, slides, email

cards.headline: Work in the order that keeps the argument intact
cards.body: Numbers first, then the insight, then the document, then the slides, then the email. Reversing that produces slides you cannot defend, because the argument was assembled to fill a layout rather than because the data supported it. Settle what the report actually claims before any of it gets formatted, and carry that one claim forward through every step so the deck and the email say the same thing as the document.
bullets: Numbers, insight, document, slides, email — in that order.
Settle the claim before anything gets formatted.
The email, the deck and the document must make the same claim.
If a step cannot support the claim, the claim was wrong, not the step.

cards.headline: Every figure in the report traces back to the source file
cards.body: By the time a number reaches a slide it has been through several hands, and nothing along the way records where it started. So hold to one rule: every figure in the report traces back to the source file, and you can point at the cell or the row it came from. Keep a short list of figure and source as you go. If you cannot trace a number by the end, it does not go in — a figure whose origin nobody can name is exactly the one a colleague asks about in the meeting.
bullets: Every figure in the report traces back to the source file.
Keep a running list of figure and source as you build.
A number you cannot trace does not go in the report.
Recalculate in the spreadsheet rather than trusting a figure in a reply.

cards.headline: An error copied forward is repeated as fact
cards.body: This is what makes a chain different from a single task. A rounding slip, a mislabelled column or a hedge quietly dropped at the first step is re-stated at the second, illustrated at the third and asserted in the covering email at the fourth — and it gains confidence at every stage, because each step is only reading the step before it. An error copied forward is repeated as fact. So check each handoff against the SOURCE, not against the previous output, and read the final email against the original numbers before you send it.
bullets: An error copied forward is repeated as fact.
Check every handoff against the source, never against the last output.
Read the covering email against the original numbers before sending.
A mistake gains confidence at each step, so catch it at the first.

cards.headline: Produce one real report end to end
cards.body: Use a report you genuinely owe someone this month, not an example. Start in the spreadsheet: settle the single claim the report makes and recalculate every figure that supports it. Then produce the document, then a short deck for the same claim, then the covering email. As you go, keep a two-column list of every figure and the exact source it came from, and at each handoff check the new version against that source rather than against the previous draft. Before you send, read the email and the deck back against the original numbers. Keep the figure-and-source list — it is what makes the report defensible when somebody asks.
bullets: "Here are the figures from my spreadsheet and the single claim my report makes. Draft the report in four parts: the claim, the evidence for it, what the data does not show, and the recommendation. Quote the exact figure and label for every number you use, do not introduce a figure that is not in what I gave you, and list anything you could not support."
Keep a list of every figure and the source it came from.
Check each handoff against the source, not against the previous draft.

quiz.question: What is the right order for building a report across the apps?
options: Slides first, then find numbers to fit them
Numbers, insight, document, slides, then the covering email
Document and email together, numbers afterwards
quiz.explanation: Starting with slides produces an argument assembled to fill a layout rather than one the data supports, and you cannot defend it when somebody asks where a figure came from.

quiz.question: A figure appears in your deck but you cannot find its source. What happens?
options: It stays in, with a note that it is approximate
It comes out until you can point at the cell it came from
It stays in if the tool produced it consistently
quiz.explanation: A number whose origin nobody can name is exactly the one a colleague asks about. Every figure in the report has to trace back to the source file or it does not go in.

quiz.question: Checking each step against the previous version is enough to catch errors in a chain.
quiz.explanation: Each step only reads the step before it, so an early slip is re-stated and gains confidence at every stage. An error copied forward is repeated as fact, which is why each handoff is checked against the source.

lessons.title: Design Your AI-Powered Workday
lessons.subtitle: Build a repeatable routine around three moments in the day — and keep the decisions that are yours to make.

cards.headline: A routine beats remembering
cards.body: Most people who learn these skills use them brilliantly for a fortnight and then drift back, because every use was a decision to make in the moment. A routine removes the decision: three fixed moments in the day where you already know what you are going to ask for. What the routine must not do is quietly take over the judgement — which is the part of your job nobody else is accountable for.
cards.statLabel: a start, a working block, a handover

cards.headline: Three moments, not thirty decisions
cards.body: Start with a short triage: what changed, what needs you, what is still open. Use a working block for the drafting and the analysis, where you brief properly and check the output rather than accepting it. End with a handover to tomorrow: what moved, what is waiting on somebody else, and the first thing you will pick up. Three moments is enough. A routine with a step for every tool is a routine you abandon in a busy week.
bullets: A start: what changed, what needs you, what is still open.
A working block: brief properly, then check what comes back.
A handover: what moved, what is waiting, what is first tomorrow.
Three moments you keep beat ten you abandon.

cards.headline: AI cannot decide what your week is for
cards.body: A tool can group your messages, summarise a thread and draft a reply. It cannot see that one client is close to leaving, that a quiet colleague is overloaded, or that the piece of work nobody is chasing is the one your year is judged on. AI cannot decide what your week is for. So the priorities stay yours: read what it surfaces as a list of candidates, not as a ranking, and pick the order yourself before the working block starts.
bullets: AI cannot decide what your week is for.
Treat what it surfaces as candidates, not as a ranking.
You set the order at the start of the day, not the tool.
The important thing is often the one nobody is chasing.

cards.headline: Never automate a decision you are accountable for
cards.body: The tempting next step is to let the routine act on its own: auto-send the summary, auto-reply to the routine request, auto-file the awkward message. Do not. Never automate a decision you are accountable for, and make sure nothing leaves you unread — your name is on it, and the recipient will hold you to it whether you read it or not. Automate the assembling; keep the sending, the committing and the declining.
bullets: Never automate a decision you are accountable for.
Nothing leaves you unread, however routine it looks.
Automate the assembling, keep the sending and the committing.
A step that acts without you is a step you cannot correct.

cards.headline: Write your own three-moment routine and run it
cards.body: Write your routine down as three short blocks: your start-of-day triage, your working block, and your handover, with the exact thing you will ask for in each. Name the decisions that stay yours in writing — what order the day runs in, what gets sent, what you agree to — and mark clearly that nothing in the routine sends anything without you reading it. Then run it for the rest of this week and change the parts that did not survive a busy day, rather than abandoning the whole thing. Keep the written routine: it is the output of this lesson.
bullets: "Help me design a repeatable daily routine with exactly three moments: a start-of-day triage, one working block, and an end-of-day handover. For each, give me the question I should ask and the output I should expect. Keep every decision about priorities, sending and commitments with me, and do not propose a step that acts or sends on my behalf."
Write down which decisions stay yours before you run it.
Nothing in the routine sends anything you have not read.

quiz.question: Why does a routine work better than deciding in the moment?
options: It removes the decision, so the skill survives a busy week
It means you can stop checking the output
It replaces the need to prioritise
quiz.explanation: Every use that requires a decision in the moment gets dropped under pressure. Three fixed moments where you already know what to ask for is what makes the habit last.

quiz.question: What should you do with the list of priorities a tool surfaces?
options: Work through it in the order given
Read it as candidates and set the order yourself
Ignore it and use your inbox order
Send it to your manager to rank
quiz.explanation: A tool cannot see which client is close to leaving or which unchased piece of work your year is judged on. AI cannot decide what your week is for, so the order stays your call.

quiz.question: Routine replies can be sent automatically once the routine is working well.
quiz.explanation: Your name is on it and the recipient will hold you to it. Never automate a decision you are accountable for — automate the assembling and keep the sending.

lessons.title: Redesign One Recurring Process
lessons.subtitle: Rebuild a process you repeat every week — and make sure it still works on the day the tool is wrong or unavailable.

cards.headline: The weekly thing you never question
cards.body: Everyone has one: the weekly update, the monthly pack, the handover, the client summary. It takes hours, the shape of it was decided by somebody who left, and you have never redesigned it because it is always due. This lesson rebuilds one of them properly — and takes seriously the part most people skip, which is what happens on the week the process is wrong and nobody notices because it always used to be right.
cards.statLabel: mapped, rebuilt, made resilient

cards.headline: Map it before you improve it
cards.body: Write the process out as it really happens, step by step, with what each step needs and who it goes to. Then mark each step as mechanical (gathering, reformatting, summarising, drafting), judgement (deciding, committing, prioritising, declining), or unnecessary. Most weekly processes lose more time to the unnecessary steps than to the slow ones. Rebuild it with AI helping only on the mechanical steps, and be honest that the judgement steps still take the time they always took.
bullets: Write the process as it really happens, not as it is supposed to.
Mark each step mechanical, judgement, or unnecessary.
Delete the unnecessary steps before automating anything.
Judgement steps still take the time they always took.

cards.headline: Check what your organisation allows before you change a process other people depend on
cards.body: This process is not only yours. Other people rely on its output, its format and its timing, and it may carry client data, personal data or commercial figures through a tool your organisation has not sanctioned. So check what your organisation allows before you change a process other people depend on, tell the people downstream what changed, and keep the output in the format they need rather than the one that suits your new workflow. A redesign nobody was told about looks like a mistake the first time the format shifts.
bullets: Check what your organisation allows before you change a process other people depend on.
Tell the people downstream what changed, before they notice it.
Keep the output format they rely on, not the one that suits you.
Remove personal and client detail from anything you paste in.

cards.headline: The process must still work when the tool is unavailable or wrong
cards.body: A rebuilt process gets trusted quickly, and that is the danger. If the tool is down on the morning the pack is due, or it produces something plausible and wrong, the process must not fail — the process must still work when the tool is unavailable or wrong. So keep the manual path written down, keep a check step that a person performs on the output every time, and make sure one human reads the whole thing before it goes anywhere. Resilience here is not caution, it is the difference between a faster process and a fragile one.
bullets: The process must still work when the tool is unavailable or wrong.
Keep the manual path written down and usable.
Keep a check step a person performs on every output.
One person reads the whole thing before it leaves.

cards.headline: Rebuild one real recurring process this week
cards.body: Pick the recurring task that costs you the most time and write out its real steps. Mark each one mechanical, judgement or unnecessary, and delete the unnecessary ones first. Rebuild the mechanical steps with AI helping, keeping every judgement step with you. Then do the two things that make it last: check what your organisation allows and tell the people downstream what is changing, and write down the manual fallback plus the check a person performs on every output. Run the rebuilt process once this week and note what broke. Keep the written process and its fallback — that document is the output of this lesson.
bullets: "Here are the real steps of a process I repeat every week, with who each step goes to. Sort the steps into mechanical, judgement and unnecessary, and say which could be removed entirely. For the mechanical ones, suggest how AI could help and what I would need to check afterwards. Leave every decision, commitment and priority with me, and tell me where this process would break if the tool were unavailable."
Check what your organisation allows, and tell the people downstream.
Write down the manual fallback and the human check step.

quiz.question: What is the first thing to do with a recurring process?
options: Map it as it really happens and mark the unnecessary steps
Ask for a summary of it
Change the format so it is quicker to produce
quiz.explanation: Most weekly processes lose more time to steps nobody needs than to slow ones. Deleting those first means you are not making an unnecessary step faster.

quiz.question: What has to be in place before you rely on the rebuilt process?
options: A manual fallback and a check a person performs every time
A copy of last month’s output to compare against
Nothing, once it has worked twice
quiz.explanation: The process must still work when the tool is unavailable or wrong. A written manual path and a human check on every output are what stop a faster process becoming a fragile one.

quiz.question: You can change a process other people depend on without telling them.
quiz.explanation: Other people rely on its format and timing, and it may carry client or personal data. Check what your organisation allows, then tell the people downstream before they notice the change themselves.

lessons.title: Capstone: Your Microsoft 365 Workflow
lessons.subtitle: Put the whole course into one real piece of work, from the numbers to the email — and keep every protection you have learned.

cards.headline: One real piece of work, start to finish
cards.body: Everything in this course has been building to this: a real deliverable you owe somebody, carried from raw material to the message that sends it, with AI helping at every step and your judgement intact at every step. Finish this and you are not holding notes about AI at work — you are holding the report, the deck, the record and the routine, and you know exactly which parts of the job never leave you.
cards.statLabel: foundations, documents, data, email, meetings, workflow

cards.headline: What the whole course adds up to
cards.body: Brief properly so the first answer is usable. Produce and reshape documents for the audience in front of you. Find the real insight in a spreadsheet and present it without overstating it. Turn a full inbox into decisions instead of a pile. Prepare, capture and confirm a meeting. Then join those into a workflow you repeat. The skills are ordinary on their own; the value is in the chain, because that is where most people still do everything by hand.
bullets: Brief properly, then check what comes back.
Reshape for the audience, never past what the evidence supports.
Turn data into one defensible claim, and an inbox into decisions.
Join the steps into something you repeat without thinking.

cards.headline: The three protections that carry this module
cards.body: Each of these prevents a failure that leaves no trace at the time. A chain re-states an early slip with more confidence at every step, so every figure in the report traces back to the source file. A routine drifts towards acting on its own, so never automate a decision you are accountable for. And a rebuilt process gets trusted fast, so the process must still work when the tool is unavailable or wrong. None of the three produces an error on the day; all three produce a problem you meet later, in front of somebody who matters.
bullets: Every figure in the report traces back to the source file.
Never automate a decision you are accountable for.
The process must still work when the tool is unavailable or wrong.

cards.headline: What never moves to the tool
cards.body: Across all six modules the same line held. You supply the context the tool cannot see: the unwritten history in the room, what a client is really worried about, what your week is actually for. You keep accuracy: figures verified against their source, names and numbers checked by hand, hedges left where the evidence is thin. And you keep the commitments: what gets sent, what gets agreed, what gets declined. Mechanical work to the tool; judgement, accuracy and accountability to you.
bullets: You supply the context the tool cannot see.
You keep accuracy: verified figures, checked names, hedges intact.
You keep the commitments — sending, agreeing and declining.
Nothing you send goes unread, however routine it looks.

cards.headline: Deliver one real piece of work using the whole chain
cards.body: Choose something you genuinely owe someone in the next week — a report, a proposal, a review, a client update. Run the full chain on it. Brief properly and settle the single claim it makes. Work the numbers and recalculate every figure, keeping a figure-and-source list so every figure traces back to the source file. Produce the document, then the short deck, then the covering email, checking each handoff against the source rather than the previous draft. If there is a meeting attached, prepare a one-page brief and afterwards capture decisions and owned actions with dates. Read everything before it leaves you, and write down the two or three steps you will now repeat every time. Send it. Then keep the deliverable, the figure-and-source list and your written routine: those three things are the proof this course worked.
bullets: "I am producing a real piece of work and I want to run it end to end. Here is the material and the single claim it makes. Give me: the questions I still need answered, a structure for the document, an outline for a short deck making the same claim, and a covering email. Quote the source for every figure, do not introduce a number or a commitment that is not in what I gave you, list what my material does not support, and leave every decision and anything that gets sent with me."
Keep a figure-and-source list so every figure traces to its source.
Read everything before it leaves you, then write down what you will repeat.

quiz.question: Where does most of the value in this course sit?
options: In joining the steps into a workflow you repeat
In producing work faster than colleagues
quiz.explanation: The individual skills are ordinary once learned. The chain is where most people still do everything by hand, so joining the steps is what changes the work.

quiz.question: Which of these stays with you in every workflow you build?
options: Deciding, committing, and anything that gets sent
quiz.explanation: Mechanical work moves to the tool. Judgement, accuracy and accountability do not: your name is on what goes out, and nothing you send should go unread.

quiz.question: Once a rebuilt workflow has run smoothly a few times, the human check can be dropped.
quiz.explanation: Trust is exactly when a plausible wrong output gets through. The process must still work when the tool is unavailable or wrong, which means keeping the manual path and the human check.
